title: Tool-call slicing and session-affinity bridge for OpenAI ChatCompletions
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Background: Several Redwood-hosted customers use the OpenAI ChatCompletions surface and expect function/tool calling behavior that maps cleanly to Redwood's tool invocation primitives. Existing compatibility layers handle simple mappings, but we have recurring issues around: (1) long-running tool calls that stream intermediate tokens, (2) request affinity when a conversation must consistently route to the same backend model instance (to preserve KV cache), and (3) idempotency when clients retry partial streams.

Goal: Implement a bridge that translates OpenAI-style 'function_call' semantics into Redwood tool invocations with:
- deterministic tool id resolution (function name -> tool id + version pin)
- streaming token slicing (emit partial tool stdout events as structured stream frames)
- session affinity hints (sticky routing keys to preserve per-session KV cache locality)
- robust idempotency semantics (client-provided idempotency token + server checkpoints)

Design summary:
1) Request translation: incoming oa-cc request is normalized and assigned: conversation_id, oa_request_id, session_affinity_key (derived from conversation_id + user_id). function_call payload is parsed; if present we translate: function.name -> redwood.tool_id (lookup table with fallback to lexical normalization). function.arguments (string) -> tool_input JSON, validated against tool schema.

2) Slicing & streaming: Redwood runtime supports streaming structured frames for tool execution: TOOL_CALL.start, TOOL_CALL.output_chunk, TOOL_CALL.complete, TOOL_CALL.error. The bridge will:
- begin a tool invocation with TOOL_CALL.start metadata pointing to the original oa_request_id and session_affinity_key.
- as the tool emits partial tokens, the runtime will emit OUTPUT_CHUNK frames. The bridge will re-encode these as incremental ChatCompletions delta events so legacy OA clients see streaming text while additional structured frames are available to Redwood-native consumers.
- on completion send a final ChatCompletions message containing the synthesized function call result object and a tool provenance header.

3) Checkpointing & idempotency: for any stream we persist minimal checkpoints (offsets + last-ack token id) keyed by (session_affinity_key, oa_request_id). Retries with same idempotency token will resume from checkpoint where possible; otherwise the bridge will reconcile by requesting a snapshot from the tool execution service.

4) Session affinity: the bridge will emit routing hints (internal header X-Session-Affinity-Key) to the smart router so that follow-up tokens in the same conversation attempt to land on the same model instance for low-latency KV cache hits. Affinity is advisory; router still respects autoscaling and capacity fallbacks.

5) Error & fallback behavior: if a tool is unavailable or schema validation fails, the bridge will:
- return an OpenAI-compatible function_call error object with a clear code and retryable=false/true flags, and
- create a synthetic assistant message explaining the failure for OA clients. For severe failures we route to a fallback sync execution path that runs the tool in a limited sandbox.

Compatibility considerations: The bridge must preserve OA wire semantics (deltas for streaming, final assistant.function_call object for completed calls) while providing richer structured frames to Redwood Console consumers and observability. We avoid mutating incoming requests beyond normalization and idempotency token enrichment.

Example mapping (simplified):
OA request snippet: {"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Get me the weather"}], "function_call":{"name":"get_weather","arguments":"{"loc": "94107"}"}}
Translated start frame -> TOOL_CALL.start: {"tool_id":"sys.weather.v3","inputs":{"loc":"94107"},"meta":{"oa_request_id":"oa-123"}}
Streaming output chunks -> TOOL_CALL.output_chunk -> OA delta frames: {"choices":[{"delta":{"content":"Sunny, 72F"}}],"index":0}

qa_steps:
1) Unit tests: mapping table coverage + invalid schema cases.
2) Integration: run bridge against local runtime with synthetic tool that emits token-by-token output; assert OA delta frames and final function_call object are correct.
3) Load test: simulate 500 concurrent sessions with session_affinity_key churn and verify p95 latency < 120ms for delta frames.
4) Chaos: kill tool worker mid-stream and verify retry/resume behavior matches spec.
5) Observability: verify Console surfaces TOOL_CALL.* events and links to OA request ids.
monitoring: Create dashboards: Bridge success rate, average checkpoint write latency, resume rate after retries, session-affinity hit ratio, and OA-compat delta latency p95. Alert if resume rate > 3% or p95 delta latency > 200ms.
rollout_plan: 1) Feature-flag behind 'oa-compat-toolcall-v1'. 2) Canary on dedicated infra for non-critical customers. 3) Gradual ramp to 25% of OA traffic, monitor errors and latency. 4) Full rollout after 2 days of stable metrics.\nFollow-ups: split affinity into 'hard' and 'soft' modes per customer SLA in a later ticket.
risks: - Checkpoint race under high concurrency (current blocker).\n- Schema mismatch for user-provided function.arguments that are non-JSON strings.\n- Affinity may reduce global packing efficiency and increase cost in tight capacity scenarios.
acceptance_criteria: 1) All unit/integration tests pass. 2) Canary metrics meet SLOs (delta frame p95 < 120ms, success rate > 99.5%). 3) No regressions in Redwood console event fidelity. 4) Documentation and SDK note published explaining idempotency token usage for OA clients.
notes: We purposely keep the OA wire format intact so downstream SDKs do not need to change. The bridge emits additional structured events to the console and internal tracing, which will aid debugging and quality regression detection. If checkpoint persistence proves too slow, fallback is to persist only per-sessionlatest-offset in memory with asynchronous flush to Redis (degrades resume guarantees).
